title: The Captain Will Not Leave (two-scene demo)

intro.text:
Your wife Mira died in the spring. She left you her ring, a debt to her brother Lazlo (he paid for the funeral, and he has not forgotten it), and the Grey Heron: a canal boat that belonged to her grandfather, Captain Lake Kaur, and has not left its mooring in the forty years since he died aboard her.

The boat has a buyer, at a boatyard four miles downstream, at noon. Sell her, and Lazlo gets his money back. He has come along to make sure you do.

The boat also has a captain. Mira used to say her grandfather never really left. You thought she was joking.

lazlo_nerve.meaning: how far Lazlo believes he can stay aboard without losing his money or his mind

captain_regard.meaning: how far the captain sees you as crew rather than a usurper

description.text: A square of tarred planks behind the cabin, slick with river damp. The tiller is lashed down with rope gone green.

exits.label: across the gangplank to the towpath
along the gunwale to the bow

description.text: Barely room for two: a brass-ringed wheel, a speaking tube, a chart drawer under the window. The windows are fogged on the inside, though nobody has breathed in here for years.

fragments.text: The chart drawer is swollen shut with damp.
The wheel has turned a quarter since you last looked, and nobody turned it.

description.text: Two bunks, a folding table, a kettle on a spirit stove, and the smell of a hundred winters. Lazlo has spread his papers over every flat surface.

exits.label: up the steps to the stern deck

description.text: Cinders and nettles along the black water. From here the Grey Heron looks smaller and older than she does from aboard, and the wheelhouse window is the only one with a light in it, though there is no lamp.
The narrow foredeck, a coil of bow line, and the boat's blunt nose.

exits.label: back along the gunwale to the stern

description.text: Thick, old hemp, knotted in a way you do not recognize. Someone tied this to last.
A frayed stub on the cleat. The other half hangs from the ring on the bank, back in its old knot, as if it had never been untied.
Lashed amidships. The lashing is newer than anything else aboard.
Brass rings worn bright in two places, where hands held it for years.
It sits a quarter-turn off true. You are almost sure it was straight.
Swollen shut. There is something heavy inside; it slides when the boat rocks.
Open now, and empty but for the smell of old paper.
Oilcloth covers, the pages ruled by hand. The entries are in a small, impatient script, the last one forty years old.

take_text.text: You tuck the logbook under your arm. Somewhere aft, a door you did not touch swings shut.

description.text: A cash book with the boat's name written on the cover in capitals. Rope, 4.50. Lock fee, 12.00. Nuisance, to be determined.
Rope, 4.50. Lock fee, 12.00. Nuisance: a figure, written carefully, and underlined twice.
Rope, 4.50. Lock fee, 12.00. The nuisance line has been scribbled out hard enough to tear the page.
The iron ring on the bank is rusted solid into its stone. Someone has painted a small white anchor on the stone beside it, many times, the newest coat not so old.
Dented, blackened, and the only thing aboard Lazlo has not priced.
A coil of rope, stiff with age but whole.

take_text.text: You heft the coil over your shoulder.

bollard.name: the bollard on the lock wall

description.text: An iron post on the lock side, a long jump from the bow.
Black oak and iron, closed, and coming closer.

lake_kaur.name: Captain Lake Kaur
lake_kaur.role: the boat's dead captain, Mira's grandfather

description.text: He stands at the wheel as if braced against a gale. When he turns his head, you see the window through it.
He stands at the wheel, and for once he looks at you the way a captain looks at crew: measuring, not dismissing.

here.text: Captain Lake Kaur stands at the wheel, looking straight ahead at nothing.
Captain Lake Kaur holds the wheel against the drift, waiting for your report.

says.text: 'The water is not ready.' He does not look at you. 'Neither are you.'
He is quiet so long you think he has gone. Then: 'I was waiting for the water to clear. It never did. You will see why.' He looks at you properly for the first time.
'First mate,' he says. 'Nine years old and she could take a lock better than I could.' The wheel creaks under his hands.

description.text: Mira's brother: a tidy man in a coat too good for a boat, with her eyes and none of her patience.
He keeps one hand on his ledger like a man holding a railing.

here.text: Lazlo stands by the cleat with his ledger open, like a toll-keeper between you and the rope.
Lazlo Brandt sits at the table with his ledger, adding up what the boat owes him.
Lazlo is at the rail shouting the price of diesel at the wheelhouse, at the ghost, as if the ghost could be billed.
Lazlo is at the rail shouting the price of diesel at you, as if you had snapped the line yourself.

says.text: He turns the ledger round so you can read it. Rope, 4.50. Lock fee, 12.00. Nuisance, to be determined. He taps the last line and waits to see what you make of it.
'Noon,' he says. 'He pays on the dock, I take what Mira's funeral cost me, you keep the rest. Simple.' He says 'simple' the way other people knock on wood.

description.text: A broad man in oilskins on the lock wall, his schedule clipped to a board and his face the colour of the brickwork.

here.text: Up on the lock wall, Pell Szeto, the lock-keeper, is shouting about his schedule and his gates.

opening.text: Before dawn, the canal is black glass. Lazlo is below in the cabin with his ledger. The stern line still holds the Grey Heron to the bank, and the light in the wheelhouse window is on, though there is no lamp in there to light.

stern_deck.text: The stern line runs from a cleat to an iron ring on the bank, the only thing holding the boat to the land.

towpath.text: Mist sits on the water so thick the far bank is a rumour.

interactions.text: You brace a foot and haul. The drawer gives with a shriek of wet wood, and a logbook slides into the light.
The last entry is forty years old and ends mid-sentence: 'Water not ready. Will wait.' As you close the cover, the wheel turns a quarter, slowly, all by itself.
Rope, lock fee, nuisance. The ledger is the only thing aboard that makes sense to Lazlo, and he knows it.
'Depends on the nuisance,' he says, and his shoulders come down an inch. He licks his pencil and writes a number beside it, carefully, like a man naming a dog so it will stop growling.
You tell him the ghost does not take payment. He laughs too, a beat late, and scribbles out the nuisance line so hard the pencil goes through.
He looks at you for a long moment, then writes today's date beside the nuisance line and closes the book. 'Later,' he agrees, in the voice of a man adding interest.

You crouch at the cleat, and before you have the first turn of the knot loose, Lazlo comes up the cabin steps with his ledger open. 'Before you do anything expensive,' he says, and holds the book out to you.
Lazlo puts his good shoe on the cleat. 'Ledger first,' he says. 'Then the rope.'
You work the old knot loose. It comes away in your hands as if it had only been waiting to be asked, and the boat stirs against the bank.

events.text: The air in the wheelhouse is suddenly cold enough to see your breath.

nudges.text: Lazlo's voice comes up from the cabin: 'Are we selling this boat or haunting it? The line, Teodor.'
Grey light finds the water. Somewhere a church bell counts six. The buyer comes at noon, and the stern line is still tied.

opening.text:
You coil the loose line on the deck and the boat slides off the bank. For ten yards the Grey Heron moves.

Then the coil leaps off the deck as if someone had snatched it, whips back across the water to the iron ring, and knots itself there in that same old knot. The boat jerks to the end of the rope, and the rope parts with a crack like a pistol shot. In the wheelhouse the wheel spins by itself. The captain has made his point: the boat leaves when he says so.

And now she is loose, swinging broadside on the current toward the first lock, whose black gates are shut. On the lock wall above them, the lock-keeper, Pell Szeto, is already shouting: you are not on his schedule, and you are about to hit his gates.

stern_deck.text: The frayed end of the line trails in the water like a fuse.

bow.text: The gates are close enough now to see the weed on them.

interactions.detail_label: 'Boat held, sir, stern to the lock'
interactions.text: You don't know the words for this, so you borrow his, the clipped canal talk he barks at the water: 'Boat held, sir. Stern to the lock.' It sounds ridiculous in your mouth. He nods once anyway, the way you would to a man who has done exactly what was asked, and the wheel stops turning. A yard short of the gates, the Grey Heron stops too.

'It stopped itself!' you shout up at the lock wall. 'It's not me, it's the boat!' Pell Szeto writes something on his board. Behind you, in the wheelhouse, the wheel spins hard once, offended, and the boat stops dead a yard from the gates.

You jump for the lock wall with the bow line. You make it, just; the rope burns through your hands as the boat swings, and from the wheelhouse a voice like a foghorn bellows 'Belay that!' The boat stops short anyway, a yard from the gates. Up on the wall, Pell Szeto looks at your hands and, slowly, offers you his.

events.text: The gates are coming. Up on the lock wall, Pell Szeto's shouting climbs half an octave.

nudges.text: From the wheelhouse, a voice like a foghorn: 'REPORT.'

text.text: The Grey Heron rides quiet in the lock, a yard from the gates. It is not yet seven in the morning.

variants.text: In the wheelhouse the captain has one hand on the wheel and the other, almost, on your shoulder.
In the wheelhouse the captain holds the course and, once, glances back at you.
In the wheelhouse the captain stands with his back to you, and the lamp you did not light goes out.
Lazlo writes 'rope, one, lost' in the ledger and, under it, 'nerve: holding'. He shows you. It is almost a joke.
Lazlo has his coat on and his ledger in his fist, and he is looking at the towpath, not at you.
Lazlo counts the diesel money twice and says nothing at all.
Pell Szeto leaves the gates open a minute longer than the schedule says.
